chapter: Touring in the bus years and Jim Crow in the South
title: Jacksonville police threaten the band at the train station
summary: A policeman tells tenor man Muse that band is no job for a Black man; Fields shelters the band on railroad property, and Jay McShann's band was arrested there later.

story.theme_name: Race and segregation in the jazz life
story.community_name: Segregation on the road and the bandstand

blocks.x: I got this white boy, and everything was going smooth and so we were in Jacksonville, Florida and I had another young man that I got, a negro out of Seattle, Washington, Muse was his name, he was a tenor player, Muse, and he was a little different from we midwest southerners; in other words, he was regular and all, but you know, we have this habit of huddling. You see one negro in a public place we all get together; and so anyway, we were in Jacksonville, Florida at the top of the peninsula, so I decided I'd talk to the driver and said I believe I checked things and I'm going by train on down to Miami and come back up on train and then stamps accumulate, you know, rations of gas, and we'll more stamps to go on.

So he checked us in after the dance, we were doing a concert there, and a Reverend King, a Methodist preacher, they change at certain times, and I had played in his church once, if not twice, on Mother's Day and they later transferred him to Jacksonville and so he
saw where we were playing there and from Oklahoma, he just says well I got to go speak to him anyway.

So he came on and he said I may not stay for everything but I don't care what they say, preacher or anything, this band is different, I got to speak to you. So he came on to the dance. So we went to the station, the valet checked everything and out little bunch was kind of in a huddle talking, and this Muse was off by himself. I'll tell you who was in the band then, Cliff Dudley.
He's here; did you see him?
Yeah, yeah, I saw him last night.
You talked to him?
Yeah.
And so Cliff Dudley--
Trombone player.
Yeah, trombone player, very nice trombone player.
And arranger.
Yeah.

So Cliff Dudley was in the band.
So anyway, we were just talking and Muse was over by himself and I noticed a policeman saying something to Muse. So after a while Muse reached in his pocket and pulled out a billfold. I figured maybe he was showing him an I.D. So Muse just paused a while and the policeman left. So eventually Muse came over to our little huddle and he said, Ernie, did you see that policeman talking to me? I said yeah, what the hell did he want? He said he acted like he was crazy. I said, what do you mean? He first wanted to know where did I work, what did I do and I think Muse told him, is that any of your business? Well, you better tell me whether you got a job, and so Muse said, well I have a job, working every night and I'm fixing now to leave on the train going to my job tomorrow night. What is your job? He said I play in a band, man. Where's the band?

There's the band over there, standing there. If you're here when I come back, I'm going to bag every one of you; that ain't no job for a nigger. So I said, my goodness, and I wondered what to do. It looked like something just told me, I found the station manager and told him what they had told this young man and he said he's right, this is city property, but I tell you what, you won't have long, it's almost train time, you'll be one of the first on and you'll be sure to get your seat. Bring your bags and things right inside this gate here and I guarantee you he won't touch you on that railroad property. And we went on in there and got inside there and we weren't in there five minutes before he went and got (inaudible).
Now where was that?
That was in Jacksonville, Florida, and that's no little town.
I've been there many times.
Jacksonville, Florida.
Then about a month later we saw where Jay McShann's band was arrested in Jacksonville, Florida and charged twenty five dollars apiece.
So then we go on--
Now, this would be during the war?
Yes.
